title: The Case of the Mixed-Up Mix
markdown:
Milo sat at the kitchen table with his brow furrowed and a pencil that had already given up. His younger siblings, Pip and Squeak, were no less puzzled.

Pip, whose sunflower-yellow hair curled like a spring, flung both hands. "But how? Mom's hair is curly. Dad's is straight, like Squeak's. Your eyes match Grandma's, Milo, and mine are like Grandpa's. We grew up in the same house. We look so different."

Squeak, whose hair was dark as garden earth, whispered, "Are we sure we're from the same family?"

Milo shook his head. "Of course we are. There's a reason. It's a Milo-style puzzle, and Milo cracks codes."

A streak of quicksilver shot across the floor. Tansy the ferret, long as a question and twice as nosy, chased a dust bunny with her nose twitching and her sharp eyes missing nothing.

"Don't worry, little explorers." The chuckle came from the doorway. Dr. Quinn, their neighbor, held a basket of ruby tomatoes. She smelled of damp earth and roses, and her spectacles caught the light. "Perhaps the garden will help untangle this."

They followed her into an explosion of color, and she stopped them at a patch of sunflowers.

"Look closely. These grew from one giant sunflower's seeds. Some stand tall, heads high. Others are shorter, bushier. Same family. Not the same height."

Milo leaned in. They were all sunflowers. They were not copies.

"Precisely," Dr. Quinn said. "You three are one family too. Inside every living thing is a set of instructions called DNA. Think of it as a book, not a single page. Each of your parents passed you half their book. Which half you got was a matter of chance, not a vote. Pip may have drawn the curly-hair instructions from Mum and a stretch of height from someone further back. Squeak drew a different mix. You, Milo, drew Grandma's eye color through one of your parents — not because the book promised it, but because that page happened to be in the half you received."

Tansy sniffed a poppy and chittered, as if the science had been obvious to ferrets all along.

"That mix-and-match is called variation," Dr. Quinn went on. "It is why you might have Mum's smile and Dad's stubborn chin, or neither, or a surprise from a grandparent. Science, not magic. Probability, not a guarantee."

Milo looked from Pip to Squeak. He saw the differences. He also saw the shared sparkle, which no one had needed a microscope to find.

"So we look different because we got different combinations," he said, grin widening. "Not because someone swapped us."

Pip bounced. "I'm a tall, big-headed sunflower!"

Squeak hummed a small joyful tune. "And I'm a short, bushy one. Still a sunflower."

Dr. Quinn's eyes invited the next step rather than a bow. "Exactly. Variation makes each living thing a slightly new experiment. Now — who wants to find more examples before the tomatoes get warm?"

Milo, Pip, and Squeak went, with Tansy prancing ahead. Milo did not file the puzzle under Solved Forever. He wondered, as they passed a row of beans that were sisters and not twins, whether a new baby in the family would look like Pip, or Squeak, or nobody they had met yet — and how you would only know after the mix had been drawn.
